title: Algorithms at medium scale
summary: 27 runs of 14 programs of well-known algorithms on up to 17 logical qubits, encoded in 113 to 699 physical qubits, on 6 hardware designs of superconducting, neutral atoms and trapped ions. Each is run through the operating system's interface on its machine's RISC-Q control system.
method: Each algorithm is a logical program. The fault-tolerant compiler lowers it to a QSysASM listing of system calls against the machine's system specification, and its resource VM admits the listing. The OS then executes every system call at its listed time on the control system, and durations the hardware needed enter the next specification until every call fits its window.

A program is compiled for each design it runs on: the design's capacities and its measured durations enter the system specification, so the same algorithm has a different listing on each. Every core runs firmware compiled from the listing in the cycle-exact model of RISC-Q; boards exchange measured bits and barriers over their PutLanes.

Atom and ion operations take microseconds to milliseconds, so their programs are smaller: one run of the Lean model covers at most 4 s of machine time, and the compiler schedules each listing within 3.3 s. Bernstein–Vazirani on 4 inputs needs 5.2 s on the QCCD grid and 5.1 s on the ion modules, and on 8 inputs 4.2 s on the moving-atom lattice (the compiler's runtime bounds), so those pairs are not run.

sections.heading: The hardware
sections.text: Superconducting, Transmons, two decoder units: a generated superconducting chip: one RISC-Q control core per transmon, each drive on its own RF-DAC, code blocks two lattice columns apart, two decoder units of 4 cores, 16,384 words of RAM per core, on as many AMD ZCU216 boards as it needs. Superconducting, Transmons, multiplexed drives, one decoder unit: a denser superconducting chip: code blocks one lattice column apart, four transmon drives frequency-multiplexed on each RF-DAC, one RISC-Q core per transmon (RISC-Q builds one readout channel into every core), and one decoder unit of 8 cores. Neutral atoms, Atoms on a 10 µm lattice, moved into gate sites: neutral atoms in tweezers on a 10 µm lattice, 16 addressed beams and 4 AODs: every route moves atoms next to their partners (ZAC's move law), one RISC-Q decoder unit. Neutral atoms, Atoms on a 2.5 µm interaction lattice: neutral atoms on a 2.5 µm lattice, where neighbours interact in place, 16 addressed beams and 4 AODs: only long-range routes move atoms. Trapped ions, QCCD grid, one ion per zone: trapped ions in a QCCD grid, one ion per zone, 16 gate beams and 32 electrode lanes: a route shuttles ions into its hub's zone (Pino et al. 2021 transport times). Trapped ions, One ion chain per code block: trapped ions with one chain of up to 64 ions per code block, 16 gate beams and 32 electrode lanes: only a merge between blocks shuttles ions.

sections.heading: The programs
sections.text: GHZ state on 12 logical qubits: 12 blocks in |+⟩ joined by a chain of Z⊗Z lattice-surgery merges into a 12-qubit GHZ state, then read out in Z. Deutsch–Jozsa on 12 inputs: 12 inputs in |+⟩ and a target in |−⟩; a balanced oracle f(x) = s·x (s = 101101101101₂) applied as lattice-surgery CNOTs from each input of s onto the target; the inputs read out in X give s, so f is balanced. GHZ state on 6 logical qubits at distance 5: 6 blocks of the distance-5 surface code in |+⟩ joined by Z⊗Z lattice-surgery merges into a GHZ state, then read out in Z. Bernstein–Vazirani on 16 inputs: The hidden string s = 1011001110001101₂ of the oracle f(x) = s·x, found with one query: 16 inputs in |+⟩ and a target in |−⟩, a lattice-surgery CNOT from each input where s has a 1, then the inputs read out in X, which give s. It is the Deutsch–Jozsa circuit with a linear oracle; Bernstein–Vazirani asks for s itself. Teleportation along 16 logical qubits: A logical |+⟩ teleported block to block along a chain of 16: each step prepares the next block in |+⟩, merges the two by Z⊗Z lattice surgery and measures the old block in X; the two outcomes set the next block's X and Z frame corrections. The last block, read out in X, gives +. Deutsch–Jozsa on 8 inputs at distance 5: 8 inputs and a target in blocks of the distance-5 surface code; the balanced oracle f(x) = s·x (s = 10110101₂) as lattice-surgery CNOTs onto the target; the inputs read out in X give s, so f is balanced. GHZ state on 10 logical qubits at distance 5: 10 blocks of the distance-5 surface code in |+⟩ joined by Z⊗Z lattice-surgery merges into a GHZ state, then read out in Z. Simon's algorithm on 8 inputs: A 2-to-1 oracle f(x) = f(x ⊕ s) with hidden s = 11010010₂: 8 inputs in |+⟩ and 8 outputs in |0⟩; the oracle copies x onto the outputs and, from input 1 (the lowest bit of s), adds s, all as lattice-surgery CNOTs. The inputs read out in X give a string y with y·s = 0; repeating the query recovers s. Teleportation along 10 logical qubits at distance 5: A logical |+⟩ teleported block to block along a chain of 10 blocks of the distance-5 surface code, each step a Z⊗Z lattice-surgery merge and an X measurement whose outcomes set the next block's frame corrections; the last block, read out in X, gives +. GHZ state on 4 logical qubits: 4 blocks in |+⟩ joined by a chain of Z⊗Z lattice-surgery merges into a 4-qubit GHZ state, then read out in Z. Bernstein–Vazirani on 4 inputs: The hidden string s = 1011₂ of f(x) = s·x found with one query: 4 inputs in |+⟩ and a target in |−⟩, a lattice-surgery CNOT from each input where s has a 1, then the inputs read out in X, which give s. Teleportation along 5 logical qubits: A logical |+⟩ teleported block to block along a chain of 5, each step a Z⊗Z lattice-surgery merge and an X measurement whose outcomes set the next block's frame corrections; the last block, read out in X, gives +. GHZ state on 8 logical qubits: 8 blocks in |+⟩ joined by a chain of Z⊗Z lattice-surgery merges into an 8-qubit GHZ state, then read out in Z. Bernstein–Vazirani on 8 inputs: The hidden string s = 10110011₂ of f(x) = s·x found with one query: 8 inputs in |+⟩ and a target in |−⟩, a lattice-surgery CNOT from each input where s has a 1, then the inputs read out in X, which give s.

findings: The largest run, GHZ state on 10 logical qubits at distance 5 on transmons, two decoder units, uses 699 physical qubits and 708 control cores on 186 boards.
Every system call of every run ran inside its window.
The longest derivation, from compile to a specification every call fits, took 32 minutes on one workstation.
